title: Gas cloud to stellar remnant
question: What decides how a star lives and ends?
hook: Every star starts as a collapsing cloud of gas, yet they do not all end the same way.
idea: A star is born from a collapsing gas cloud, shines by fusing hydrogen, and its total mass mainly decides how it ends.

beats.prompt: Two stars form from similar gas clouds, but one has far more total mass. What should you expect about their lives?

choices.label: They will follow the same path and end the same way
choices.feedback: Similar clouds sound like similar outcomes, but a star's total mass mainly determines its evolution and eventual fate.

choices.label: Their evolution and fate will differ, since mass mainly sets them
Only the lighter one will ever fuse hydrogen into helium
choices.feedback: Fusing hydrogen into helium is how a star shines for most of its active life, so it is not limited to one of them.

beats.explain: A star's total mass mainly determines its evolution and eventual fate.

beats.prompt: Put these star-watching records in order, oldest first.
items: Aristillus makes the first Greek star catalogue (about 300 BC)
Hipparchus's catalogue lists 1,020 stars (2nd century BC)
Chinese astronomers record a supernova (185 AD)
The brightest recorded stellar event, SN 1006, is seen (1006)
beats.explain: Aristillus worked around 300 BC, Hipparchus in the 2nd century BC, then came the supernova of 185 AD and SN 1006.

beats.prompt: Match each process to what it does.
pairs: Powers a star for most of its active life
Creates almost all elements heavier than lithium
Returns enriched material to the interstellar medium
Mainly determines a star's evolution and fate
beats.explain: Each process plays a part in a star's life, from shining to feeding new generations of stars.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: A star begins as a collapsing gaseous nebula.
In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium and releases energy.
So when fusion ceases, every star's core becomes a white dwarf.
Material returned to space can be recycled into new stars.
beats.explain: The core may become a white dwarf, a neutron star, or, if the star is massive enough, a black hole.
